rationale: A wins because it keeps the story sharp without freelancing beyond the fact block. Its strongest line, "The FDA has flagged compounded GLP-1s. Hims & Hers is scaling them anyway," is grounded, beat-specific, and immediately testable. B has real bones, but "Novo Nordisk Spent Years Building the GLP-1 Market" imports named companies and history the update did not give it; that is how a useful angle turns into a fact-check problem before the first email goes out.
gaps_in_A: "With at-home blood tests, telehealth moves from writing prescriptions to running diagnostics" is viable, but close to overclaiming unless Hims can show the test changes prescribing or dosing decisions.
"Hims & Hers just turned profitable" slightly sharpens "recently turned profitable" into a cleaner narrative than the facts strictly prove, though it stays inside the line.
A could have called out that "a fraction of branded-drug prices" is unusable until converted into monthly dollar figures earlier and harder in the affordability angle.
gaps_in_B: "Novo Nordisk Spent Years Building the GLP-1 Market" invents named manufacturers and a market-history frame not supplied in the update. True in the real world is not the assignment; grounded in the brief is the assignment.
"Eli Lilly" and "Novo Nordisk" are introduced as targets without support from the provided facts. The update only says branded manufacturers pushed back.
"branded manufacturers have lobbied against compounders" upgrades "pushed back" into a specific tactic. That is not a harmless flourish; it changes the story.

Refusing "At-home lab testing as a standalone digital health trend angle" is too timid. The update explicitly gives blood testing as a new service; the right move is to pitch it with proof gates, not throw it out.
